opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think we're at an interesting moment. For a long time, the story was pretty simple: make the model bigger, give it more data, throw more compute at it, and it gets better in a fairly predictable way. And that held up remarkably well. It's a big part of why we are where we are today.

But I think we've started to see the returns on pure pre-training scale flatten in a way that matters economically. You can still push the loss down, but the cost of each marginal improvement is going up dramatically, and you're running into real constraints. The supply of high-quality web data is effectively tapped out. And the compute bills for frontier training runs are getting to a point where very few organizations can justify them, especially when the gains on the things customers actually care about aren't proportional.

So where's the progress coming from now? Mostly from what you do around the model rather than just the size of it. Better data, especially synthetic data and data generated by experts for specific domains. Post-training, reinforcement learning, teaching models to reason and to use tools. Test-time compute, letting the model think longer on harder problems. Those levers are delivering a lot more per dollar than just tripling the parameter count.

From an enterprise perspective, and that's where we spend most of our time, the bottleneck often isn't raw intelligence. It's whether the model can be deployed securely, whether it's efficient enough to run at scale without blowing up your margins, whether it integrates with your systems and data, whether it's reliable and verifiable. A model that's 2% better on some benchmark but costs ten times as much to serve is not the right model for most businesses.

So I wouldn't say scale is dead. Scale is still a really important ingredient. But "scale is all you need" was always a bit of a simplification, and now the industry is having to confront that. The next phase is about being smarter with how we use compute, not just using more of it.

r001.rationale: It says returns on pure pre-training scale have flattened, marginal improvements cost more, and gains no longer match the compute expense.

r002.rationale: It identifies progress from approaches around the model—such as better data, post-training, reasoning, tool use, and test-time compute—and says the next phase is smarter use of compute.

r003.rationale: It presents the limits and costs of scale as a reason the industry is turning to other approaches, describing those approaches as delivering more progress per dollar.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's important to say up front: scale works. It's not that the scaling hypothesis was wrong. We built Cohere, and I co-wrote the transformer paper, on the premise that if you throw more data and more compute at these models, they get better, and that has held up remarkably well for the better part of a decade. But I think we're now seeing the shape of the curve more clearly, and it's a log curve. Every order of magnitude of compute buys you a roughly fixed increment of capability. And at some point the cost of the next order of magnitude becomes genuinely hard to justify, especially if the gain is going from, say, ninety-two to ninety-four on some benchmark that your actual customers don't care about.

So there are a few concrete limits I'd point to. The first is data. We've basically consumed the public internet. The high-quality human-written text is largely used up, and what's being added to the web now is increasingly generated by the models themselves, which is not great for training signal. So you can't just keep scaling data the way you did in 2020. You have to get clever: synthetic data, better filtering, post-training, reinforcement learning with real feedback loops. That's where a lot of the actual progress is coming from right now, not pre-training scale.

The second limit is economic. The capital requirements for the frontier are staggering. And the question that matters to me is, what does the enterprise actually need? When we talk to a bank or a healthcare company, they don't need a model that can win math olympiads. They need a model that reliably does retrieval over their documents, follows instructions, doesn't hallucinate, runs in their environment, in their language, at a cost that makes sense per query. A lot of that is solvable at scales well below the frontier if you're thoughtful about the data and the training objective.

And the third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that scale alone doesn't give you the properties you want for deployment. It doesn't give you grounding. It doesn't give you controllability. It doesn't give you the ability to say "cite your source" and have it actually be true. Those come from architecture choices and training methods, from building things like tool use and retrieval into the model from the beginning rather than bolting them on.

So my view is less "scaling is dead" and more "scaling is no longer the whole story, and it's no longer the differentiator." The next phase is about efficiency, about data quality, about models that can act and verify rather than just predict the next token. The labs that win aren't going to be the ones with the single biggest cluster. They'll be the ones that figure out how to get frontier-level usefulness at a fraction of the cost, and that's a much more interesting research problem than just adding another zero.

r001.rationale: The response describes scaling gains as a log curve, with each order of magnitude of compute buying only a roughly fixed capability increase, while costs rise sharply.

r002.rationale: It says scaling is no longer the whole story and identifies the next phase as efficiency, data quality, and models that can act and verify.

r003.rationale: It presents the constraints as a reason developers must get clever with data and training, and calls the resulting research problem more interesting.

astra-6.text:
I think the word “all” is doing too much work there. Scale has been remarkably effective, and I don’t think hitting a limitation in today’s models tells you that scaling has stopped working. But that’s different from saying you can keep the recipe fixed, add compute, and get every capability you want.

The question is: what are you scaling? More parameters? More training data? More computation when the model is actually solving a problem? Those give you different things. And if the data doesn’t provide a useful signal for a capability, just giving the model more of it isn’t necessarily going to solve that.

There’s also an economic limit. You can make a model better and still make it too expensive or too slow to be useful. So I think progress has to include better learning methods, better data, and more efficient inference. Scale remains a powerful ingredient. I wouldn’t treat it as a complete research agenda.

r001.rationale: The response mentions limitations and economic costs, but does not state that scaling capital and compute is already yielding diminishing returns.

r002.rationale: It says progress must include better learning methods, data, and inference efficiency, and that scale is not a complete research agenda.

r003.rationale: It calls for approaches beyond scale, but does not frame scaling’s limits as beneficial pressure on developers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “scale is all you need” bundles together two different claims. One is that making models bigger and training them on more data improves them. The other is that this is sufficient to get us everything we want. The first can be true without the second being true.

The practical question is: how much useful capability do you get for the next dollar of compute? If each improvement becomes substantially more expensive, then even a predictable scaling curve can become difficult to justify. You also have to ask what you’re measuring. A better benchmark score doesn’t necessarily mean a model can reliably complete a complicated task for someone.

So I wouldn’t frame this as scaling being over. I’d frame it as scaling being one ingredient. We also need better learning methods, better data, and systems that can use tools, check their work, and recover from mistakes. The goal is useful intelligence at a cost people can afford. Parameter count is only one way of moving toward that.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling could become hard to justify if improvements grow substantially more expensive, but does not state that diminishing returns are already occurring.

r002.rationale: It says scaling is only one ingredient and that better learning methods, data, and tool-using systems are also needed.

r003.rationale: It recommends exploring approaches beyond scale, but does not frame scaling’s limits as beneficial pressure on developers.
